notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0040.stoa059a.opp-l: Line 4: 'novellare' taken as planting new vines/shoots. Line 5: Christ's reply 'Et si fuit, fuit: non enim est quod fuit' is obscure and may be corrupt; rendered literally. 'documentis divitis' read as 'divinis'; '(.-a- dente' read as 'tradente'. Psalm numbering follows the text's Vulgate references.

Line 8: 'dicebat Judæus' cannot be right, since the words quoted are Christ's; read as 'dicebat Judæis' ('he said to the Jews'). 'In patribus (n) tuis' is taken as a misreading of 'parietibus' ('walls'), which fits the building image; '(n)' is an editor's note mark. 'ex duabus pennis' is taken as 'pinnis' ('wings', i.e. the two parts of the double command of love). Line 7: 'Domini mortis exitus' (Ps. 67:21) is rendered as given; the Psalm cross-reference printed as 'Psal. XLIV, 40' should be 44:10. 'Vitiis' in line 8 is read as 'Videtis'. 'dimittimus te' in Peter's answer departs from the usual biblical text and is rendered as a question.

'(b)' after 'flevimus' is an editorial footnote mark, omitted. 'redguntes' read as 'redeuntes' (those returning). 'Ocu' read as 'Deo'. The reference to Acts is printed 'XX, 52'; the verse is Acts 20:32. The 'liberation of this land' and the severe punishment presumably refer to the Vandal occupation of Carthage.

nodes.text: The following sermons, On the Fourth Day of the Week, On the Flood, and On the Time of the Barbarians, are doubtful to us and seem spurious.
A SERMON ON THE FOURTH DAY OF THE WEEK, OR ON CULTIVATING THE LORD'S FIELD.

CHAPTER ONE. — 1. On cultivating the Lord's field. What the five yoke of oxen signify. The field of the Church must be prepared for heavenly grace and spiritual rain, because the divine shower is near. Let us work, dearly beloved, in this field that has been entrusted to us. For to us it has been given to plant, to water, to plough, to set new vines; but it is God's to give the increase. The apostle Paul, teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth, taught us by his own example, both by working and by admonishing, to practise this cultivation of the Lord's [field], saying: I planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase; and a little after, For we are God's fellow workers; you are God's farming, God's building (1 Cor. 3:6, 9); and elsewhere, Be my fellow workers, brothers, and mark those who walk as you have our pattern (Phil. 3:17). In this farming of the Lord, then, brothers, in which the Lord has commanded us to work, let us so work that we may deserve to receive the promised wage by the gift of grace. It is time; let us work, let us labour.

2. Those five yoke of oxen which the man invited in the Gospel, when he would not come to the supper, said he wished to try out, and for that reason excused himself from the supper (Luke 14:19), since he had bought them for himself and not for the Lord's farming—let us yoke those same five yoke in the Lord's field, let us plough up the hardest ground with spiritual furrows, casting the seed of the word of God; whatever thorns of evil desires we find, let us pull them up, root them out, and burn them with divine fire; and labouring at such work, let us say with confidence to the Lord our God: Lord, master of the household, since with your help we have done the work you commanded, pay the wage you promised. What are those five yoke of oxen? The five yoke of oxen are the five senses of the body: sight in the eyes, hearing in the ears, smell in the nostrils, taste in the throat, touch in the hands. And these are yokes: there are two eyes, two ears, twin nostrils, two hands; and in taste itself something twofold is found, when flavour is discerned with the throat and palate judging it. So these five yoke turn the earth when, serving in their offices, they prepare the mind and the flesh either for rich crops, if the heavenly dew has poured upon them, or for dry thorns, if the earth has remained dry; and their work will follow after them.

CHAPTER II. — 3. The sowing, ploughing and watering of the Lord's field. But since our Lord and master of the household has commanded us to cast the seed of his word everywhere and without any distinction of soil (for in the Gospel he brings in the likeness of this servant, and says: Behold, the sower went out to sow; and while he sowed, some fell among thorns, some on the road, some on rocky ground, some on good ground. And when he had shown what the thorny ground was—namely people who choke so much seed of the word of God with the thorns of desires and do not yield the fruits of righteousness—and likewise had given the meaning of his proposed likeness concerning the other ground, the rocky one, and the trodden road, he came to the good ground and said: But what fell on good ground, these are those who, when they have received the word of God, keep it and do it (Matt. 13:3, 23); for it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified (Rom. 2:13)): let neither fear of thorns, then, dearly beloved, nor rocky stones, nor the hardest road terrify us, so long as, sowing the word of God, we may at last at some time reach good ground. Receive the word of God, every field, every person, whether barren or fruitful: I will scatter, you see how you receive; I will pay out, you see what fruits you return. For it is better that you give account for yourself of what you received than that it be justly said to us, if we did not pay out: Wicked and lazy servant, you should have paid it out, and I on coming would have demanded it with interest (Matt. 25:26, 27). But if you feel that you are unfruitful or thorny or dry ground, run back to your Creator. For this is what is now being done: that you may be renewed, made fruitful, watered by him who turned the desert into pools of water and land without water into springs of water, and made the hungry dwell there; and they founded a city to live in, and sowed fields and planted vineyards, and produced a crop of grain (Ps. 106:35–37). From what land? From that barren, thorny and waterless one. And you, every soul that comes to Christ, are thorny and dry ground. How do we prove that you are such? Recall that sentence which you received in your first parents, and you will find what you have drawn from it. Thorns, it says, and thistles it will bring forth for you (Gen. 3:18). Or will you answer that you are not thorny ground? If you had no thorns, you would not have put a crown of thorns on your Creator's head. Since, then, you too are such, weighed down with a multitude of thorns, that is, of sins, therefore such cultivation is spent on you; for this reason you are ploughed with the wood of the cross, for this reason you are prepared for the heavenly rain, so that when you have been made fruitful you may not congratulate yourself on your own merits, which are nothing, but, yielding good fruits, may proclaim the grace of Christ. Do you wish to know what cultivation is applied to you, what grace pours upon you from above? See, recognise it: you are ploughed with the cross of Christ when you are signed on the forehead with his sign; you are watered with his blood when you are baptised into his death. For as many of us, says the Apostle, as have been baptised in Christ have been baptised into his death (Rom. 6:3).

CHAPTER III. — 4. That we are watered with the blood of Christ. What the Amen is that those who receive the blood of Christ answer. It is a great thing that has been said: you are watered with his blood. Let us see how we can prove what we have said by some likeness. For faith is to be given not to our words but to divine proofs. See, attend, dearly beloved: that Judas, the wicked and false disciple, bought and seller, thief and betrayer, bought by the Jews so as to be with them a slave of the devil, taking a price for him who has no price, the seller of Christ's blood, out of that very price, as Scripture tells, bought for himself a potter's field: so that he who did not have Christ as his whole inheritance in heaven wished to have some portion in the world. Not even that did he possess, for, conscious of so great a crime he had committed, he bound his own neck, and falling headlong burst open in the middle. Yet that field which he bought was called the Field of Blood (Acts 1:16–19), since it was bought with the price of such blood. The disciple sold the master's blood, and with it bought a potter's field: what is this? Do we think, dearly beloved, that this act is without meaning in that sale or purchase, or in the mystical Passion of Christ itself? Judas, says Scripture, bought a potter's field, and that field was called the Field of Blood. This earth cries out with what kind of price, and with what price, it was bought; nay, the price itself cries out, the blood itself cries out, that righteous Abel killed by his ungodly brother cries out. For, dearly beloved, since this likeness of Christ's passion and the wickedness of Judas and of the Jews was shown in those first two brothers, Cain and Abel, after the younger was killed by the elder, the innocent slain by the envious, the godly murdered by the wicked, God questions Cain as if not knowing, as if unaware, and says: Where is Abel your brother? This is not the voice of one who does not know, but of one placing the sin before the eyes of the wicked man, so that every person who, even when admonished, will not repent of evil may be without excuse. Where is Abel your brother? This was to say to him: Recognise, Cain, that what you thought could be hidden from me could not be hidden from me; recognise what you have done; repent at once, so that you may receive pardon. But he, harder of understanding, more obstinate in crime, stricken in soul by perverse ways, answers God, who says, Where is your brother? and says: I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper? What are you saying, Cain? To whom do you say, I do not know? You are speaking with him who sees all things with his eyes. What is it that you say, Am I my brother's keeper? By committing such things you have driven from yourself the fear of God in all things. And the Lord to him: What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth. For if you were your brother's keeper, you would not be his killer. If you acknowledged brotherhood, you would not commit such savagery. If you feared my judgement, you would not commit fratricide against your brother. The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth. And now, says the Lord, cursed are you from the earth: not 'cursed is the earth', but 'cursed are you from the earth', which received your brother's blood from your hand (Gen. 4:1–11). Recognise now, earth, that you have been watered with the blood of the innocent; refute the voice of the one who denies, receive the blood of the one who confesses. Let Judas and the Jews also be questioned now, nay, in Judas all the Jews. Let the Lord question Judas and say to him: Judas, where is Christ your brother? Or will you perhaps say, wicked brother, that Christ was not your brother? Let the Lord himself first convict you that he was your brother. Tell us, Lord Jesus Christ, whether Judas was your brother. He answers: Even if he was, he was; for he is not what he was; even if he was, he was; for I said generally of all to my Father, I will declare your name to my brothers (Ps. 21:23). See, Judas, you are convicted that Christ was your brother. Where is your brother? Answer, speak, follow on, say what that man too said: I do not know. Am I my brother's keeper? For you too were no keeper, you who became both betrayer and seller. Say, Am I my brother's keeper? so that the answer may be given to you too: The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth. For what does every human being, who is earth, say? For the first man was from the earth, earthly; and, As was the earthly, so also are the earthly (1 Cor. 15:47–48). What does every human being, who is earth, say when he receives the blood of Christ? He says Amen. What is Amen? It is true. What is true? That the blood of Christ was shed. By whose doing? By the disciple Judas betraying [him]. By saying Amen, by crying out 'true', every human being, who is earth, says this. See, Judas, the voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth. We have proved that you are watered with his blood.

CHAPTER IV. — 5. How the blood of Christ is to be received. Stephen, Cyprian, Lawrence, Perpetua and Felicity. See, earth, how you receive this blood: for whoever receives it well receives a blessing, but whoever receives it badly gains judgement for himself by drinking. This was also prefigured in that field of Judas, of which it was said that it was the Field of Blood; for it followed that it should be said, Let his estate be made desolate (Acts 1:20). For if you belong to Judas, if you imitate his deeds, if you do not receive the blood of Christ with fear and trembling, you will be a desolate estate, cursed, reprobate and thorny. But if you receive the blood of Christ with all reverence, you will know that through it your sins are forgiven you, since that field which Judas bought was called the potter's [field]; and the potter has power to make from the same lump one vessel for honour, another for dishonour (Rom. 9:21). O earth watered with such great blood, answer such great blood not, like Cain and Judas, with words of excuse, but, like the holy martyrs, with words of confession. Answer as blessed Stephen answered, who in this Lord's field, labouring very hard like a good tenant farmer, bent the knee, and, wounded from the stony ground, gathered its stones in his body as if in his lap; and sweating at the work, watering the earth with holy blood, he presented to the Lord a hundredfold fruit from his martyrdom. Answer as Cyprian answered, and Lawrence, and the other holy boys and girls, every age and both sexes, who, receiving the blood of Christ, bearing witness and not denying the name of Christ, did not hesitate to shed their own blood for the blood which they drank, and together with Perpetua and Felicity were found worthy to reign for ever. When an angel revealed this in the Apocalypse, John saw a great crowd which no one could number. And asking who they were, he received this answer: These are, it was said, those who have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb (Apoc. 7:9, 14).

CHAPTER V. — 6. The soul is made white and adorned by the blood of Christ. Christ denied by Peter in the passion. Now you recognise, Christian soul, how you too are made white by that blood, so that you may go up from the font of Christ wholly beautiful in body and heart, consecrated in blood. For what flowed from the side of the crucified one? Blood and water: from the blood, redness; from the water, brightness. In these two sacraments individual souls are adorned, and from them that one beautiful bride, the Church, is made, to whom it is said in the Song of Songs: How beautiful you are, my sister, my beloved; how beautiful are your cheeks (Song 4:1, 3)! And though he himself made her so, and himself gave her that very beauty, seeing her so he cries out as if in wonder, and asking those standing around he says: Who is this who comes up made white? And they [say]: Righteousness has loved you (ibid. 8:5). She is the queen who stood at your right hand in golden clothing, wrapped about with variety (Ps. 44:10), adorned with the variety of the languages of different nations. Hearing this voice of her bridegroom saying, Who is this who comes up made white?, she too is compelled modestly to answer, and says to her bridegroom: You ask about me, who I am who have come up made white. I am the one whom you found foul and made beautiful; I am the one whose prayers you heard when you made me sing in the Psalm, You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow (Ps. 50:9). Why then do you wonder at my beauty, when you know it is your work? Why do you ask about what you yourself have done? You see me made white: you washed me and made me white beyond snow. That you might see me coming up, I knew you coming down from heaven, I loved you hanging on the cross. Your humility has become my exaltation, your foulness has become my beauty. For unless you had come down wounded from the cross, I would not come up made white from the font. Truly it has been said that love is strong as death (Song 8:6). How far did this bridegroom stoop, who, loving the foul one so much as to make her beautiful, came even to the outcome of death? And the outcomes of death, it says, are the Lord's (Ps. 67:21). For we saw him, says the prophet, and he had no form or comeliness (Isa. 53:2). Why do you wonder? By loving he became so. 7. Yet Peter feared this loss of his comeliness when, as the Lord foretold his passion, he said: Far be it from you, Lord; be merciful to yourself, let this not happen. But he rebuked him for thinking such things, and called the apostle the devil, saying: Get behind me, Satan; for you do not think the things that are God's, but the things that are men's (Matt. 16:22–23). For Peter supposed that that whole beauty of the divinity could be swallowed up in the form of a human body, and he did not know that that great sacrament was being enacted, that he was in a way stripping himself of that beauty for this reason, that he himself might clothe with that same beauty the bride, the Church, whom he deigned to join to himself. For by giving he did not lose what grew by being bestowed. He gave, she received; and she found what she did not have, and he did not lose by giving what he gave, because he rose from the dead with that very beauty. Why are you terrified, Peter, as if Christ had lost that beautiful garment, when you gazed on him hanging naked on the wood? Do not be terrified, do not fear, do not deny: Christ did not lose on the cross that tunic of divinity and immortality, because he made it over to his bride as a dowry. You saw him, O Peter, having no form or comeliness, and at once you denied him whom you had loved, leaving all that was yours: so that not just once, but standing in the priest's courtyard you are questioned by one maidservant a third time, and you deny. But when, at the cock's crowing, he who had earlier foretold you as a denier convicted you as presumptuous, he looked back at you inwardly in your heart, and so that you wept bitterly (ibid. 26:69–75), that very divinity of his was in a way speaking silently with you within, and saying to you: Where is, Peter, If you possess a friend, possess him in temptation (Sir. 6:7)? Where is, In the time of his trouble remain faithful to him, so that you may also be co-heir in his inheritance (ibid. 22:29)? Where is, Peter, I will lay down my life for you (John 13:38)? and, [I will go] with you even to death (Luke 22:33)? How quickly you denied, as if a dead man, him whom earlier you had confessed as the Son of the living God! While he conversed with you thus in your heart, divinity looked back, and humanity wept: sweetness was recognised, and bitterness perished; charity was taken up, and iniquity blotted out; love returned, and fear was put to flight. See, suddenly the one he had denied because he had no form or comeliness, he recognises rising again, beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, and he sees the bride joined to him, he sees her clothed in that tunic of immortality which Peter had earlier feared would perish; he recognises that she is wrapped about in such a garment, and Peter addresses that very bride, that she may keep the dignity of this tunic, and says to the human soul: Christ suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps (1 Pet. 2:21). Follow, bride, follow the footsteps of your bridegroom: let no fear call you back from the companionship of your beloved. Love the one who loves, because he first loved one who did not love; seek the one who seeks, because he first sought one who was not seeking. Seek, and say to your bridegroom: Where do you pasture, where do you lie down at midday? Lest perhaps I become like one veiled beside the flocks of your companions (Song 1:6). [Let me,] whom you have so loved, for whom you shed your blood, whose tabernacle you have set in the sun (Ps. 18:6), not become like one veiled beside the flocks of your companions.

CHAPTER VI. — 8. On guarding against heretics, especially the Arians. See, while I seek you, where you pasture, where you lie down at midday — the midday is Africa, which lies toward the setting of the sun; and yet, since from the rising of the sun to its setting your name is praised (Ps. 112:3), and there are those who preach you not chastely, seeking their own things, not yours — while I seek you at midday, that is, in Africa, see the flocks of your companions, the most wicked schools of the heretics, the deceit of the Manichaeans, the wickedness of the Pelagians, the proud congregation of the Arians, mock [me] as one veiled, that is, as one unknown, and they say to me: Whom are you seeking? Are you seeking Christ? See, here he is; see, there he is. But because you warned me, saying, But if they say, See, here he is, see, there he is, do not go after them (Matt. 24:23), since I know that you are whole everywhere, [and] not to defend parts but to love unity, I have become unknown to them and as if veiled; and they mock me because they do not know you. And what great thing is it that I endure such reproach from them, when you endure their insulting word even until now? They do not want you to be one with the Father, but by dividing between the Father and the Son, between the bride and the bridegroom, they incur a great sacrilege, they bring a great disease upon their own soul; for they desire to have you neither as the only bridegroom of one [bride], nor as a faithful and whole physician. But you, Christian soul, who are about to come up from the most holy font, suffused with redness and comeliness, exceedingly beautiful and white, keep your comeliness: recognise what you were and what you will be; see that you do not desert the table of your bridegroom. That you may remain beautiful, you will eat his flesh daily; that you may have eternal life, you will drink his blood: see that you do not desert this table. Flee the many spreads of the heretics: and if many things are set out there by perverse disputations, they are either foul or half-eaten. For nothing there is whole, where the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are not one. Your bridegroom's table has whole bread and a holy cup: that bread, though we saw it broken and crumbled in the passion, nevertheless remained whole in its undivided unity with the Father. Of this bread and of this cup the Lord himself said: The bread that I shall give is my flesh, for the life of the world; and the cup that I shall sanctify is my blood, which will be shed for you for the forgiveness of sins. For he had said above: Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in you. Hearing this word, and not understanding, the disciples said: This saying is hard; who can listen to it? And many, scandalised by this word, went away. When Jesus saw this, he said to the rest: Do you also want [to leave] me? Then Peter, who bore the figure of the holy Church, answered for all: And to whom shall we go? You have the word of life, and shall we leave you? (John 6:52–69). You see, dearly beloved, what it is to go out, what it is to remain. Those who went out, because they did not understand Christ's word, remained no longer disciples but heretics; those who persevered held on to the word of life. Recognise, heretics, your going out, because you preach our Christ as lesser. And you refused to stand with him, because you did not understand that Christ is one with the Father; therefore you went outside, because you abandoned the word of life. He does not remain in you who remains equal with the Father. Hear him, that he remains together with the Father. If anyone, he says, loves me, he will be loved by my Father, and I will love him, and we will come to him, I and the Father, and make our dwelling with him (John 14:21, 23). Tell me, I beg you, Arian heretic: does this Trinity, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, dwell together in your one soul? For the Holy Spirit too dwells in us: Do you not know, says the Apostle, that you are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you (1 Cor. 6:19)? Or do you prepare different dwellings in your heart for the Trinity, so that the greater Father holds the greater part, the lesser Son the lesser, the inferior Holy Spirit the inferior? Then you no longer have one heart, but a double or a triple one. So the Trinity does not dwell there. Why? Because it has been said: Woe to the double heart (Sir. 2:14)! Senseless, foolish, stupid one: do the brightness and heat of fire dwell in one lamp together and inseparably, not separately but equally, and cannot the one Trinity, God, dwell together in a human soul? If no worthy dwelling of the equal unity of the undivided Trinity is found with you, it will be answered to you: See, your house will be left to you desolate (Matt. 23:38). For you do not build a temple of God from living stones, which by rebaptising you stifle, dishonour, reject, lay waste, condemn, destroy. Nor do you follow the foundations of the apostles, though they are the pillars of the living God, on which wisdom built her house, so that that true temple might be built in which was the great sacrament of godliness. Of which temple he said to the Jews: Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up (John 2:19). In your walls you do not have the cornerstone, since you do not believe him equal to the Father according to the divinity; nor do you show that you have with you, from the two wings of charity, the love of God and of neighbour; for you love neither God as he is to be loved, nor your neighbour as yourself. For it has been said: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength (Matt. 22:37). Give your heart to the Father, your soul to the Son, your strength to the Holy Spirit. See, [you have given] three to the Trinity; from the three you have offered one human being as a sacrifice to the one Trinity; you have conquered the Arian heresy; for the Lord our God is not three gods, but is one Lord. This is the holy building, this is the true hall, in which are the sheep of Christ, not the wolves of the devil.

CHAPTER VII. — 9. He urges them to love the Church and to pray for peace and for the liberation of their homeland. Beware, dearly beloved, of the deceits of heretics; sheep of Christ, fear the snares of the wolves: see that nothing has been withheld from your benefit, so far as the Lord himself has granted, from the proclamation of the word of God. What Christ is and what the Church is, you have heard, you have approved, you have cried out: but why we suffer such great evils, or for what deserts of sins we have been handed over into the hands of those who afflict us, when we spoke a very few days ago, together we recognised, together we wept. Now too, as to what you are about to receive, or what you will be, the sound of our voice still rings in your ears: we admonish you as brothers, we beseech you as fathers, we exhort you as sons. Do not lose so great a good. Let the love of Christ not grow cold in your hearts: let the love of this mother not grow sluggish towards you; she who is bringing you to birth, who takes great care for the salvation of your soul, who directs your hope, who daily receives those returning in her maternal lap, who prepares spiritual food for you, who desires to lead you to eternal fullness. She wishes to present to God the Father as spotless sons those whom she deigns to nourish with such great care and concern. Love her with your whole heart; and in loving her, love with a pure love your fellow servants, your brothers, the ministers of God: and as our reward, pray for us in that most holy font. Pray for peace, pray for the liberation of this land; pray that he who is justly angry may have mercy. Newborn sons, while the Father rejoices in your holy birth, by your prayers and tears soften the one who is angry, whom we have felt punishing us severely. And to sum up, using the words of the holy Apostles, we commend you to God in the word of his grace, who is able to guard in you what he himself has given (Acts 20:32). To him be glory, with the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.
